A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching algorithms, benchmarks, and retained appendix tables. The text and appendices are readable. However, v4 Figure A6 largely fails to display the ImageNet-R forgetting trajectories visible in v3 Figure A.5, limiting comparison of those per-task results.

before.justification: v3 reports original classification experiments, including accuracy, forgetting, blurry-task comparisons, and aggregation analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains original benchmark experiments and adds results concerning large output vocabularies with dummy labels, including detailed appendix tables.

M1.justification: The Cosine Classifier and PEFT Ensemble retain their substantive update and inference procedures. However, v4 adds label remapping beyond v3's filtering procedure and introduces private label discovery using binary DP mechanisms, including noisy-count thresholding (Section 4.3 and Appendix C.4). These substantially expand the procedures available for selecting output labels.

E1.justification: Both versions use Split-CIFAR-100, Split-ImageNet-R, and 5-Datasets, including the retained blurry-task variants. The added dummy-label experiments vary the classifier's assumed output vocabulary on existing data; they do not introduce another dataset, domain, or classification task.

E2.justification: The Non CL Baseline appears in v3 Figure 5's output-label comparison but is absent from the corresponding comparisons in v4 Figures 3 and A2 and Table A3. The benchmark baselines, last-layer comparisons, and aggregation-rule comparators elsewhere are retained.

E3.justification: v4 adds output-vocabulary configurations with 10×, 100×, and 1000× dummy labels at epsilon 1 and 8. The label-space study no longer includes v3's non-DP comparison. The retained benchmark protocols preserve the backbone, task counts, metrics, 40 training epochs, and 20 hyperparameter-tuning trials.

E4.justification: v3 compares exact task-label priors against the full benchmark label set. v4 additionally tests robustness to large numbers of labels that never appear during training (Figures 3 and A2). This substantially extends validation of the public-vocabulary assumption. The existing blurry-task and aggregation-rule analyses remain.

E5.justification: v4 Section 7 explicitly states five repeats, their variability sources, and min/median/max plotting across experiments; Table A3 specifies five-seed mean and standard-deviation summaries for label-space results. v3's explicit repeat information was concentrated in benchmark and aggregation captions. This broadens disclosure without establishing an increase in runs.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantive dummy-label findings and detailed label-space and blurry-task results. For example, Table A3 reports 64.76±1.23% for PEFT on ImageNet-R at epsilon 8 with 1000× dummy labels, a condition absent from v3. Retained benchmark tables are numerically unchanged. However, new Table A4 does not reconcile with Figure 4, and the missing trajectories in Figure A6 cannot establish numerical changes.

T1.justification: v4 generalizes the filtering proposition to label remapping, derives a group-privacy bound on dropping small classes, and adds private label-release definitions, theorems, and proofs in Appendix C.4. Appendix B.1 replaces v3's Cartesian-product adjacency construction, while Appendix D.4 adds composition guarantees when multiple task datasets differ. Existing composition theorems are also relocated.

C1.justification: v3 presents public label knowledge as required and emphasizes task-wise DP and two classifier methods. v4 offers both prior-based and privately learned labels, and makes two new central claims: very large prior vocabularies can incur little utility loss, while private label discovery risks discarding small classes (abstract, introduction, and conclusion).

C2.justification: v4 explains privacy-budget splitting and rare-class loss under private label discovery, supports using large taxonomies, and discusses hierarchical or unknown-label remapping. It also attributes blurry-task PEFT degradation to unequal data across ensemble members. The limitations shift from knowing classes and extending to open-world learning toward bounded tasks and difficulties with online or task-free learning.

D1.justification: v4 Appendix E.4 adds hardware, memory, feature caching, runtimes, and approximately 30 GPU-days of resource usage. Existing implementation libraries, hyperparameters, and access information remain. Conversely, the ImageNet-R description ends at '80/20', losing the completed train/test-split explanation and 41–334 samples-per-class detail present in v3 Appendix H.

R1.justification: v4 adds Dinur and Nissim (2003) and Lin et al. (2024), including discussion of stronger DP synthetic-image methods. It removes several citations, including Gao et al. (2023), Pelikan et al. (2023), and Radford et al. (2021). The core positioning against earlier DP continual-learning definitions and label-space practices remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. Label-space privacy now precedes task-wise formalization, and label-space experiments precede domain-shift experiments. The appendices are reorganized with a contents page; the standalone DP-SGD background and empty appendix heading are removed.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Figure 1 is redrawn, v3 Table 1 is removed, a class-dropping bound plot is added, benchmark plots are merged, and new label-space tables and blurry-task distribution panels appear. v4 Figure A6 also loses most visible forgetting trajectories from v3 Figure A.5.

improvement.justification: v4 improves the treatment of label selection through private alternatives, robustness evidence, and reproducibility details. However, new Table A4 reports PEFT i-Blurry accuracy of 57.73±13.46% at epsilon 1 while Figure 4 retains a median near 80%, without reconciliation. v4 also loses visible forgetting trajectories and part of the ImageNet-R split description. These substantive gains and reporting regressions leave the net quality change uncertain.
